newsitem.title: FRANCE: Future French cabinet faces Telecom sale decision.
newsitem.headline: Future French cabinet faces Telecom sale decision.

text.p: Whatever the outcome of the French election on Sunday, the future government will have to decide rapidly whether or not to go ahead with the sale of shares in France Telecom.
"My feeling is that the sale will go ahead but later in the year," said a Paris-based analyst.
"Everything is in place, it's just waiting for the word go. It would be a waste if it were delayed," another London-based analyst said.
The outgoing government of Prime Minister Alain Juppe had planned to sell a 35 percent stake in June with an aim of raising 30 to 50 billion francs.
The Initial Public Offering (IPO) of France Telecom could be the biggest French share market operation ever with financial analysts putting a value of 160 to 210 billion francs on the group.
"We await the outcome of the election," said a spokeswoman at France Telecom SA.

The Socialist Party's position remains unclear. It has said it opposes some privatisations and appears to be keeping its options open on partial stake sales, but financial analysts say a left-wing government may be forced to sell a minority stake anyway.

The position of a new centre-right government would depend on the name of the prime minister, with some commentators saying National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin might be a less ardent supporter of the sale than Juppe.

The more socially-oriented Seguin and ultra-liberal former finance minister Alain Madelin have emerged as a new tandem in the centre-right government's campaign following Juppe's announcement that he will stand down.
Madelin is a staunch supporter of market liberalisation and privatisations.
Aides to Seguin were not immediately available on Friday to comment on his views about France Telecom but financial analysts expected him to support the partial sale.

"He may be anti-Europe and against liberalisation but the law about the liberalisation of telecoms in France has been passed and I do not see why he would have any qualms about the sale," the London analyst said.
"Any centre-right government would go ahead with the sale, and on time, absolutely," said the Paris analyst.
The position of a left-wing government would depend on the make-up between the Socialist Party and the Communist Party. The Communists are squarly against the sale.

The Socialist Party is leaving its options open, vowing not to privatise France Telecom and saying it will consult France Telecom staff before deciding. While it opposes privatisation it is not clear if this policy would always cover minority stake sales.
"I doubt that if Jospin carries out the promised poll of France Telecom staff that the sale can go ahead before, say, the first quarter of 1998," said the analyst in Paris.

"Such a poll could be done rather quickly, I think, I don't see why this should delay the operation. The market conditions are good at the moment, the pre-marketing is as good as done and you do not know what the market will be in six months' time," said the analyst in London. Both analysts declined to be identified.
The revenues from a France Telecom sale cannot be used to cut the budget deficit as France aims to meet the Maastricht Treaty criteria for European Monetary Union (EMU).

The outgoing government planned to use the revenues to offset the cost of capital injections to other state owned companies -- Credit Lyonnais, GAN, Thomson Multimedia, GIAT -- that would otherwise have weighed on the budget.
